Triggers.value: Specific body parts associated with the event
Night-time or waking up in the dark

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Going to sleep or lying in the dark

Memory.value: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

issues.item: Escape Route Planning: always plan an escape route before entering a place
issues.explanation: 'Always plan an escape route before entering a place' implies a persistent current external-danger / entrapment threat style that is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which centers on intrusive sensory memory linked to the child's illness (body parts, darkness, songs; reliving, fragments, present-tense memory). For trauma of a child's life-threatening illness, this strategy is clinically much less coherent than avoidance/sleep delay, and it is not supported by any Threat or Appraisal items. Given the formulation, Triggers and Memory are strongly linked, but this item reflects a different syndrome focus (situational escape/safety behavior) not represented elsewhere in the selected nodes.

vignette: Kiet's world was turned upside down when his seven-year-old daughter, Linh, was rushed to the hospital with a life-threatening illness. The memory of her frail body, hooked up to machines and monitors beeping incessantly, still haunts him. He recalls the feeling of helplessness as he watched doctors and nurses scurrying around her bedside, their faces etched with concern. The image of Linh's pale face, her eyes sunken, and her tiny hands grasping his finger is forever seared into Kiet's mind. As a farmer, Kiet is accustomed to the rhythms of nature, but since Linh's illness, he has found himself avoiding the quiet darkness of nighttime. He stays up until the early hours, scrolling through his phone or watching TV, trying to distract himself from the memories that flood his mind when the house grows still. The sound of certain songs, ones that were playing in the hospital waiting room or during the long drives to and from treatments, can instantly transport him back to those terrifying days. Even the sight of specific body parts - the fragile curve of a child's neck, the delicate shape of small hands - can trigger a cascade of emotions. When these memories resurface, Kiet feels like he is reliving the event all over again. The feeling of being trapped in that hospital room, powerless to help his daughter, threatens to overwhelm him. Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear, leaving him disoriented and on edge. As a result, Kiet has started avoiding people, afraid of being triggered by conversations or situations that might remind him of Linh's illness. He finds it difficult to connect with his wife, who is struggling to understand why he is pulling away from her. Kiet's avoidance behaviors have become a self-reinforcing cycle. By staying up late and avoiding sleep, he feels like he can keep the memories at bay, but this only leads to increased fatigue and irritability. His relationships with his family are suffering as a result, and the isolation is exacerbating his feelings of guilt and shame. The triggers that were once manageable have become more potent, and Kiet finds himself becoming increasingly withdrawn. As the days turn into weeks, Kiet's world has shrunk to the confines of his farm. He avoids going into town or attending community events, afraid of encountering people who might ask about Linh or show him pictures of their own children. The memories that once felt like they were receding into the past now feel more present than ever, and Kiet is desperate for a way to break free from this cycle of avoidance and fear. Kiet's wife has been encouraging him to seek help, but he is hesitant, afraid of confronting the emotions he has been trying so hard to avoid. The prospect of reliving the memories of Linh's illness in therapy terrifies him, but he knows that he cannot continue living like this. As he looks out at the fields he once loved tending, Kiet feels a sense of despair wash over him. He is trapped in a never-ending cycle of fear and avoidance, and he doesn't know how to escape.
